Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Emerging contaminants (ECs) pose escalating global threats to water security and human health, driving urgent demands for advanced remediation; however, electrocatalytic elimination of trace ECs remains intrinsically constrained by dual limitations: diffusion of ultra-dilute pollutants and sluggish interfacial electron transfer. Here, we introduce an integrated strategy that synergistically regulates mass transport and electron transfer using a conductive molecularly imprinted polymer (c-MIP) electrode operated in a charging-discharging mode. The c-MIP selectively enriches trace ECs at the electrode surface, overcoming diffusion barriers. Critically, its capacitive properties enable temporal control of electron delivery, synchronizing the electron transfer rate with the intrinsic oxidation kinetics of ECs during the discharging phase. This synchronization achieves near-complete EC degradation with 90% lower energy consumption than conventional direct-current electrocatalysis, while maintaining 99% (95% Confidence Interval: 98.0%−100.0%) efficiency over 1,000 cycles. Our work delivers an energy-efficient electrocatalytic platform with operational stability for advanced trace organic pollutant remediation.

---

## Introduction

With the explosive growth of emerging contaminants (ECs) stemming from industrial production and consumer activities, their potential ecological toxicity has become a significant global concern1–5. Although ECs are typically present at trace concentrations, their risk quotients often exceed safety thresholds due to extremely low Predicted No-Effect Concentration, resulting in high ecological risks6–9. In wastewater treatment plants, conventional approaches such as biodegradation and adsorption/membrane filtration are commonly employed for EC removal. However, these methods face significant limitations, including low degradation efficiency and the inability to achieve complete mineralization10,11. Electrocatalysis has emerged as a reliable and adaptable means for advanced water purification12,13. However, its practical application in EC removal is hindered by high energy consumption14. In most cases, substantial overpotentials are required to achieve a satisfactory removal rate, which in turn leads to exponential growth in both energy consumption and carbon emissions15. These challenges underscore the urgent need for innovative electrocatalytic strategies that address both energy efficiency and degradation efficacy.

A key bottleneck in current electrocatalytic systems (Fig. 1) arises from the extremely low concentrations of ECs in wastewater, typically in the ppt-ppm range16–20. Under such conditions, mass transfer of EC molecules from the bulk solution to the electrode surface becomes rate-limiting. Enhancing local reactant concentrations at the electrode-electrolyte interface is therefore critical. Moreover, even if the limitation in mass transfer was overcome, the sluggish electron transfer kinetics in EC degradation also impede performance according to our results. Conventional direct current (DC) electrocatalysis typically expends significant energy overcoming electrode polarization and sustaining undesired side reactions, leading to poor overall energy efficiency21–23. Thus, breaking the limitations in both mass transport and electron transfer simultaneously is the key to improve the energy efficiency of electrocatalytic EC removal.

Selective enrichment of ECs at the electrode surface represents a promising strategy to alleviate mass transport limitations. While many existing strategies focus on overcoming mass transport limitations through selective enrichment, the equally critical constraint of electron transfer kinetics has been largely overlooked. Conventional approaches such as interfacial functionalization or pre-concentration membranes offer limited benefits in enhancing electron transfer process. The integration of molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) and non-potentiostatic electrochemical operation mode offer a compelling solution by simultaneously addressing both challenges. In addition to the high selectivity of MIPs that increases local concentrations of ECs24,25, their porous structures also contribute considerable capacitive properties, allowing them to store electrical energy in the form of non-Faradaic charge within the electrical double layer26–30. Beyond the considerable capacitance, certain long-lived organic radicals formed during catalysis may also contribute to continued contaminant degradation24,25,31. Effectively harnessing this energy presents a novel route to enhance performance and reduce energy input. Therefore, when integrated with appropriate electrochemical operation modes, MIPs can function as electrochemical reservoirs that accumulate charge during DC polarization and gradually release it during the discharging stage. This controlled energy release aligns well with the inherently slow kinetics of EC degradation, thereby enhancing electron transfer efficiency and reducing overall energy consumption.

In this work, we introduce a “charging-discharging” electrocatalytic strategy coupled with a conductive MIP (c-MIP) to synergistically regulate the electron delivery and optimize energy utilization during EC degradation. Using azithromycin (AZN) as a model contaminant, the system achieves significant mineralization in both charging and discharging phases, delivering ~90% energy savings compared to conventional DC electrocatalysis, as confirmed by in-situ CO2 evolution monitored via differential electrochemical mass spectrum (DEMS). Additionally, the system exhibits excellent operational stability, maintaining 99% performance after 1000 cycles. Overall, this work provides a dual-mode electrocatalytic platform that synergistically integrates molecular imprinting and pulse-like energy delivery, offering a scalable, selective, and energy-efficient solution for real-world EC removal in water treatment systems.

---

## Results

Preparing the c-MIP
A thiophene-based c-MIP was prepared using functional monomers as shown in Fig. 2a. It is worth noting that benzo[1,2-b:5,6-b′]dithiophene-4,8-dione (Bth-BQ) was adopted as a redox-active catalytic center to facilitate the direct electron transfer. The electron microscopy images (Supplementary Fig. 1) supported the successful synthesis of c-MIP. To avoid the use of organic reagents like methanol and acetic acid in traditional template extraction32,33, multiple electrochemical extraction methods, potentiostatic, cyclic voltammetry, and redox pulsing, were explored. Then Fe(CN)6 3−/4− was adopted as the redox probe to evaluate the amount of AZN combined with MIP before and after each treatment, as the absence of AZN would improve the accessibility of electrodes to Fe(CN)6 3−/4−. As displayed in Fig. 2b, the reduction peak of Fe(CN)6 3− was suppressed before extraction due to the occlusion of surface sites by AZN. The reduction peak rose after all 5 procedures, and the redox pulses switched between 1.2 V for 30 s and −1.0 V for 30 s (Fig. 2c) performed best as the peak current boosted most. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) corroborated these findings. The Nyquist plots of the MIP (PBth-BQ)@GCE before and after pulsed extraction differed a lot (Supplementary Fig. 2a). By fitting parameters with the equivalent-circuit model shown in Supplementary Fig. 2b, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) of MIP dropped from 4358.0 ± 98.8 Ω to 60.9 ± 7.0 Ω after extracting AZN templates by the redox pulse, indicating a more accessible interface for electron transfer. Also, the fitted n dropped from 0.92 ± 0.01 to 0.63 ± 0.02 after extracting templates, indicating enhanced surface porosity34.

To further confirm the successful imprinting and removal of AZN, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis was conducted. A prominent absorption at ~1630 cm−1, corresponding to the C=O stretching of AZN35, was present in the MIP before extraction and disappeared following redox pulsing (Fig. 2d). Upon rebinding AZN, the C=O peak re-emerged, verifying the selective recognition capability of the MIP without structural degradation. As revealed by contact angle measurements, an improved hydrophilicity was achieved after polymerization, decreasing from 89.1 ± 3.9° to 43.2 ± 2.3° (Fig. 2e), which is expected to promote aqueous-phase contaminant capture36. Also, a thin and uniform MIP layer is crucial for the selective recognition and rapid adsorption of target ECs, as the uptake process primarily follows a Langmuir-type mechanism involving monolayer adsorption onto a limited number of imprinted sites. An excessively thick MIP layer may hinder the direct electron transfer between the captured ECs and the underlying electrode surface by increasing charge transfer resistance and limiting access to electroactive sites. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis confirmed a uniform film morphology with a thickness of approximately ~7 nm (Fig. 2f, g), indicating a favorable two-dimensional configuration for electron transport37,38. The AZN adsorption isotherm on c-MIP (Supplementary Fig. 3) showed a maximum adsorption capacity (qm) of 16.35 μg/cm2 and demonstrated a Langmuir-type adsorption behavior (R2=0.99), which indicated a single layer adsorption. As a result, the adsorption kinetics tests demonstrated the rapid and high-capacity uptake of AZN by the MIP (PBth-BQ)@GC electrode that it adsorbed 8.4 times more AZN than bare GC in 10 min and 6.8 times more in 240 min (Fig. 2h).

Identifying electron transfer limitation of ECs beyond mass transport
To identify electron transfer behaviors of typical ECs in electrochemical oxidation, we employed Fourier-transform alternating current voltammetry (FTacV) to evaluate five typical ECs: AZN, carbamazepine (CBZ), tetracycline (TET), amoxicillin (AMX), and ciprofloxacin (CIP). The ECs are dripped on the glassy carbon electrode (GCE) to avoid diffusion limitation. The total current, AC voltammetry (ACV), direct current voltammetry, and 3rd harmonic components extracted from FTacV measurements on a bare GCE in the presence and absence of each EC were displayed in Supplementary Figs. 4–9. Generally, the 3rd harmonic ACV excluded the contribution of non-faradic current and decoupled overlapping electron transfer processes, thereby offering deeper insights into the redox behaviors of these ECs. Notably, the 3rd harmonic ACV current responses recorded at varying frequencies (0.19–47 Hz) suggested the difference in electron transfer rates of these ECs39,40.

Among the ECs tested, AZN, a macrolide antibiotic of significant environmental concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial activity41, exhibited the slowest electron transfer kinetics. At a high frequency of 47 Hz, AZN displayed a weak oxidation signal between 0.5 and 1.0 V (Fig. 3a). However, as the frequency decreased, the oxidation peak increased markedly, suggesting a strong dependence on electron transfer rate42. This trend reflects the sluggish redox kinetics of AZN, which is further corroborated by the monotonic increase of normalized third harmonic current (I3/f) with decreasing frequency. A similar trend was observed for AMX, CBZ, CIP, and TET, indicating that electron transfer limitation is a common bottleneck in the electrochemical oxidation of ECs. These observations collectively suggest that most ECs in wastewater are characterized by inherently slow interfacial electron transfer processes. Meanwhile, their trace concentrations (ppt-ppm) impose significant mass transfer limitations, reducing the flux of reactants to the electrode surface. These two limitations act in concert that the insufficient delivery of ECs exacerbates the already sluggish electron transfer kinetics, resulting in low overall reaction rates. As a result, in conventional electrochemical degradation systems, only a small portion of the input electrical energy contributes directly to pollutant removal, while the majority is dissipated to overcome polarization and maintain the electric double layer. Recognizing the dual constraints imposed by mass and electron transfer, we selected AZN, a typical macrolide antibiotic (ML), as a representative EC due to its environmental relevance and characteristically slow degradation kinetics, which enables a focused investigation of strategies aimed at improving electrocatalytic performance and energy efficiency.

Overcoming the mismatch of electron flow with sluggish electron transfer of ECs
To elucidate the potential of discharging induced degradation of ECs, DEMS was employed to monitor the real-time evolution of gaseous products near the working electrode. As shown in Fig. 4a, the relative intensity of CO2 increased steadily during the potentiostatic “charging” phase (applied for 300 s), indicating active mineralization of AZN under applied potential. Control experiments (Supplementary Fig. 10) confirmed that the origin of the CO2 signal. In the absence of AZN, the CO2 intensity decreased by 96%, verifying that the detected CO2 primarily arose from AZN mineralization rather than background sources. A minor residual CO2 signal was attributed to the decomposition of the Vaseline used for sealing the DEMS cell. Intriguingly, during the subsequent “discharging” phase under open-circuit, the CO2 signal continued to rise transiently despite the cessation of external voltage. This delayed decline (Δt≈30 s) in CO2 intensity implies that the stored charge within the porous electrode or the electrical double layer sustained further mineralization of AZN even in the absence of an applied potential. To further validate this coupling between stored charge and continued degradation, a series of time-dependent experiments were conducted following different durations of the charging phase (Supplementary Fig. 11). In particular, a brief closed-circuit pulse (0 V, 1 s) was introduced after potentiostatic charging to consume the stored charge, and a sharp decrease in CO2 intensity was observed. This confirms that the stored electrical energy in the electrode and interfacial regions could be effectively released to drive continued AZN mineralization during discharging stage.

To demonstrate the compatibility of c-MIP with the charging-discharging operation mode, its capacitive characteristics were thoroughly investigated. Capacitance fitting based on EIS (Supplementary Fig. 12) revealed a film capacitance (Cfilm) of 2701 ± 773 μF and an electrical double layer capacitance (CEDL) of 12.2 ± 1.4 μF. Differential capacitance analysis by cyclic voltammetry attributed most of the increased faradaic capacitance to quinone groups (Supplementary Fig. 13), whereas PBth-BQ contributed minimally to non-faradaic capacitance. The substantial enhancement in total capacitance (Fig. 4b) was attributed to the porous MIP structure, as supported by BET analysis that the specific surface area increased from 3.28 m2/g to 47.25 m2/g, and pore volume also rose markedly (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15). To further clarify the origin of capacitance enhancement, the total capacitance was deconvoluted into pseudocapacitive and EDL components and correlated with surface area and pore structure (Supplementary Fig. 17). After electropolymerization, the surface area decreased, and CEDL declined due to the coverage of the dense polymer layer, while a distinct pseudocapacitive response emerged from the introduced quinone redox sites. After extracting templates, both the surface area and pore connectivity increased, accompanied by a pronounced rise in CEDL and a moderate increase in Cpseudo. The pore-sized distribution was centered around 2.6 nm, within the mesopore range, consistent with the enhanced ion-accessible channels that promoted double-layer formation. These trends indicated that the enhanced pore accessibility mainly promoted double-layer formation, while the pseudocapacitance was controlled by the density of exposed redox-active sites. Moreover, the adsorption capacity normalized by surface area exhibited a consistent increase, supporting that improved pore connectivity facilitated pollutant enrichment and charge utilization (Supplementary Fig. 17f). Impressively, the MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC electrode delivered superior continuous discharging performance. As shown in Fig. 4c, discharging curves were collected for various electrodes after a 60-s potentiostatic charging step in 0.1 M Na2SO4. The modification of PBth-BQ resulted in a slower decay in voltage, indicative of enhanced charge retention or higher capacitance. Notably, the discharging duration was significantly extended even in low-electrolyte conditions (0.005 M Na2SO4), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18. Furthermore, kinetic analysis of PBth-BQ yielded a discharging rate constant (k0’) of 0.216 s−1 (Supplementary Fig. 19), supporting its long-lived redox activity. Moreover, this strategy was validated on alternative substrates, that PBth-BQ and MIP(PBth-BQ) also significantly enhanced the discharging behavior of titanium-based electrodes (Fig. 4c), highlighting its general applicability. Thus, the conductive and porous nature of MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC not only promotes selective AZN adsorption but also acts as temporary energy reservoirs for sustained contaminant degradation. This dual role supports a charging-discharging electrocatalytic degradation pathway, whereby more electrons are stored during the charging stage and subsequently released in a sustained manner during discharging, enabling effective degradation of MLs.

Equipped with capacitive c-MIP, we conducted a series of charging-discharging experiments for energy-efficient pollutants removal. As illustrated in Fig. 4e, the electrode adsorbed approximately 50% of AZN within 1 h via selective binding to imprinted cavities. Upon subsequent DC electrolysis at 1.2 V, 98% of AZN was effectively degraded. Surprisingly, a cyclic “charging-discharging” mode, which introduced a 2-min discharging stage after each charging cycle, achieved comparable removal efficiency to the continuous DC mode, despite reducing the total “circuit-on” time by 66.7%, indicating substantial energy savings. By employing denser sampling during the discharge period, we further confirmed that AZN was substantially degraded in the discharging stage itself (Supplementary Fig. 20a). In contrast, a control charging-pulse procedure that disabled the discharging phase (gray line in Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 20) resulted in much lower removal rates, underscoring the critical role of discharging-associated catalysis. The discharging curves remained stable over 80 cycles, with OCP decreasing gradually from 1.2 V to 0.9 V (Fig. 4d). The subtle change of OCP caused by AZN (Supplementary Fig. 21) suggested that the adsorption of ECs had little effect on the discharging processes. The high efficiency of AZN degradation at lower potentials was corroborated by differential pulse voltammetry (DPV, Supplementary Fig. 22), showing superior activity of MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC over bare GC, attributed to both enhanced AZN enrichment by the MIP and efficient direct electron transfer facilitated by Bth-BQ. The degradation activity exhibited negligible decline even as the OCP decreased to 0.9 V, implying the limited electron transfer in electrochemical oxidation of ECs. Further insights from Supplementary Fig. 23 confirmed that AZN oxidation primarily occurred between 0.7 and 1.4 V, aligning with DEMS data (Supplementary Fig. 24), where CO2 evolution initiated at 0.7 V and remained stable between 0.9 and 1.2 V, supporting sustained mineralization of AZN in the discharging phase.

In terms of durability, the electrode retained its electrochemical capacitance over 1000 continuous charging-discharging cycles (Fig. 4f), and maintained structural integrity throughout a 14-day accelerated lifetime test. Detailed capacity retention behavior over 1000 discharging cycles, as well as FTIR, XPS, and SEM analyses before and after extended cycling, are provided in Supplementary Figs. 25 and 26, confirming the long-term stability of the c-MIP electrode. Nyquist plots and fitted parameters (Rct and n, Supplementary Fig. 27b, c) further validated the long-term stability of the c-MIP architecture. To assess the limits of electron utilization, a prolonged discharging protocol, a 19-min discharging period followed a 1-min charging cycle, was employed, in which the OCP declined from 1.2 V to 0.6 V (Fig. 4g). Although the degradation rate constant decreased at lower potentials, the final AZN removal remained high. In 12 full cycles, the terminal discharging potential stabilized, demonstrating consistency in performance. While the charging-discharging electrocatalysis displayed slightly slower kinetics than DC electrolysis, the final removal rate was comparable (Fig. 4h). In contrast, the gray curve (charging-discharging 3#) concentrated all charging periods at the beginning rather than distributing them cyclically, thereby losing the benefit of alternating charge-discharge regulation and resulting in weaker degradation efficiency. The gray controls in Fig. 4e and h, though configured differently, showed the same discharge suppression and similarly reduced performance. These results collectively confirmed that the cyclic distribution of charging and discharging stages was essential for maintaining high removal efficiency. To further verify the effectiveness of this process at the mineralization level, total organic carbon (TOC) and ion chromatography (IC) analyses were performed. TOC and AZN concentrations decreased simultaneously in the initial adsorption stage (Supplementary Fig. 29), confirming rapid enrichment by the c-MIP electrode. During the charging-discharging stage, TOC exhibited a short-term increase that may be attributed to the release of oxidized intermediates into solution, followed by a steady decline as these species were further degraded. After 5 h, 79.0% ± 2.6% of TOC was removed (95% CI: 74.1%–83.9%), and IC analysis confirmed the absence of NO3−, suggesting substantial mineralization of AZN. LC-MS further indicated that key intermediate products of AZN exhibited reduced toxicity (Supplementary Figs. 30 and 31). Strikingly, energy consumption was dramatically lower that DC electrolysis consumed 35.85 ± 0.55 C to degrade 97.6 ± 0.17% of AZN in 5 h, whereas charging-discharging electrocatalysis achieved 96.7 ± 0.01% degradation using only 3.76 ± 0.19 C, or 10.5 ± 0.4% (95% Confidence Interval: 9.4%–11.6%) of the energy required by the DC mode (Fig. 4i and Supplementary Table 3). The substantial energy savings primarily stem from the synergistic contribution of the c-MIP and the charging-discharging operation, where electrical energy is stored temporarily at the charging stages and then released at the discharge stages, emulating reservoir-like energy redistribution. This process effectively reduces energy dissipation that would otherwise be spent on sustaining electrode polarization and maintaining the electric double layer in continuous DC systems.

To further examine the practical applicability of c-MIP coupled with charging-discharging electrocatalysis, the removal of AZN was tested in lower concentrations and in real water samples. C-MIP captured 45.2, 68.5, and 86.7% of AZN in 60 min when the initial concentration were 5 ppm, 1 ppm, and 0.5 ppm, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 32). At lower initial concentrations, c-MIP coupled with charging-discharging electrocatalysis achieved more effective AZN removal, in which selective adsorption demonstrated remarkable capability of selective adsorption for rapidly enriching the target analyte, especially from dilute solutions. In real water samples, the enrichment of AZN by c-MIP was slightly affected, as the removal rate within 60 min decreased from 47.2% in synthetic water to 36.3% and 40.3% in two real water samples (Supplementary Fig. 33a). This decline can be attributed to the interferences from natural organic matters containing hydroxyl groups. The selectivity of c-MIP toward AZN over other three coexisting ECs in real water was also examined, where c-MIP maintained a high selectivity of 75.6%–87.0% (Supplementary Fig. 34). The charging-discharging processes were also influenced in real water, with lower OCP values during discharging process compared with synthetic systems (Supplementary Fig. 34b), which may be attributed to the low conductivity of real matrices. Consequently, the final AZN removal rate after 5 h decreased from 96.7% in synthetic water to 86.2% and 88.5% in real samples, while electricity consumption also dropped from 3.76 ± 0.19 C to 0.39 ± 0.06 C and 0.48 ± 0.01 C, respectively, indicating high energy efficiency.

Furthermore, the c-MIP platform was extended to validate its capability for selectively enriching diverse ECs. For ECs containing hydroxyl groups like TET, a c-MIP was constructed using 3-TBA as the functional monomer, enabling the formation of boronate ester bonds with hydroxyl groups of TET (Supplementary Fig. 35a). The resulting c-MIP exhibited strong selectivity toward TET (Supplementary Fig. 35b), with minimal interference from DCF and SMX. Similarly, for ECs containing carboxyl groups like DCF, 3,4-diaminothiophene (3,4-NH2-Th) was employed as the functional monomer to form amide bonds (Supplementary Fig. 35c). Although its overall efficiency was slightly inferior to the c-MIPs developed for MLs and TET (Supplementary Fig. 35d), these results confirm that amide bond formation is a viable strategy for imprinting carboxyl-containing contaminants. However, targeting amino-group-containing ECs such as SMX proved more challenging. A c-MIP prepared with 3,4-thiophenedicarboxylic acid as the functional monomer was designed to form amide bonds with SMX (Supplementary Fig. 35e), while the resulting polymer failed to effectively distinguish SMX from TET (Supplementary Fig. 35f). This reduced selectivity can be attributed to the slower kinetics of amide bond formation with amino groups, while TET, bearing multiple hydroxyl groups, rapidly formed stable boronate esters, thereby outcompeting SMX and dominating the binding sites. Taken together, these results indicated that the c-MIP strategy can be readily adapted by tailoring template molecules and selecting complementary functional monomers, thereby enabling selective enrichment of ECs containing hydroxyl or carboxyl functional groups.

To address safety concerns in large-scale applications, specifically the instantaneous current surge associated with constant-voltage (CV) charging, a constant-current-constant-voltage (CCCV) protocol was adopted, inspired by battery technologies43. A cut-off potential of 1.65 V was set to avoid oxygen evolution, as determined by LSV analysis (Supplementary Fig. 36). A constant charging current of 0.07 A was identified as optimal, taking ~20 s to reach the cut-off voltage (Supplementary Fig. 37). Compared to the CV-only method, which reached a peak current of 380 mA, the CCCV protocol peaked at a much lower 70 mA (Fig. 4j), reducing surge-related risks while maintaining degradation performance (Supplementary Fig. 38). Leveraging this optimized procedure, we scaled up the system to a 5 L reactor to assess practical feasibility (Fig. 4k). Despite the increased volume, efficient AZN degradation with low energy input was maintained (Supplementary Fig. 40). The slight drop in removal efficiency was primarily attributed to mass transfer limitations stemming from suboptimal mixing. The radar chart displayed in Fig. 4l summarizes the comprehensive advantages of c-MIP and pulsed electrocatalysis across multiple performance indicators. Compared to PBth-BQ-modified electrodes, the c-MIP system demonstrated superior adsorption capacity, selectivity, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, charging-discharging electrocatalysis outperformed the DC mode in terms of cycling stability and power economy. Although pulsed electrocatalysis has been explored in contexts such as CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR)44–47 and redox-active electrode stability48,49, its application of “charging-discharging” as a strategy for energy-saving electrocatalysis remains largely unexplored. Our work pioneers this approach, demonstrating that the synergistic integration of c-MIP and charging-discharging electrocatalysis can significantly break the binary constraints of mass transport and electron transfer when addressing trace ECs, offering a promising paradigm for sustainable environmental remediation.

Mechanism of the efficient electrocatalytic removal of targeted ECs
To elucidate the underlying mechanism behind the efficient and energy-saving electrocatalytic degradation of MLs, we further examined the mass and electron transfer dynamics of charging-discharging electrocatalysis using c-MIP electrodes. We first evaluated the targeted mass transfer behavior of c-MIP by testing five ECs. Namely, three target MLs, AZN, roxithromycin (ROX), and clarithromycin (CLA), and two common interferences, TET and CBZ. As shown in Fig. 5a, the c-MIP electrode selectively enriched the targeted MLs from the bulk solution, confirming its molecular recognition ability. To further clarify the driving factors enabling dilute contaminants to approach the electrode surface, adsorption experiments of AZN were conducted under different stirring rates (0–1000 rpm) and initial concentrations (0.5–10 ppm). Higher stirring rates significantly accelerated adsorption kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 41), indicating that external mass transfer was important in dilute systems, while the adsorption capacity increased with concentration, confirming the concentration gradient as the primary driving force. These results provided direct evidence supporting the effective enrichment of trace pollutants by c-MIP electrodes, beyond the molecular recognition effect. More importantly, beyond these generic effects, c-MIP provided a unique advantage over conventional adsorption materials. The imprinted sites can form reversible covalent linkages with target molecules, enabling rapid capture and suppressing desorption, thereby shifting the adsorption-desorption equilibrium toward efficient enrichment. To understand the interaction at a molecular level, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to estimate the binding energies between thiopheneboronic acid (TBA) and the three ECs (Fig. 5e). Among them, AZN exhibited the strongest binding affinity with TBA at −5.34 eV, which likely arises from the boric acid-cis-diol interaction, a highly specific covalent interaction. This selectivity was further reinforced by the “lock-and-key recognition” effect inherent to the spatial structure of the MIP matrix50. Although TET and CBZ also formed interactions with TBA, their calculated binding energies were weaker than that of AZN, yet still stronger than non-specific adsorption on graphite (−0.81 eV), possibly due to boric acid-hydroxyl group bonding.

Second, to probe the electrochemical degradation in the charging stage, in-situ DEMS was employed. During LSV, the evolution profiles and LSV currents of MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS and bare CS were compared (Fig. 5b). MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS showed significantly higher current between 0.7 and 1.4 V, correlating with the earlier onset and higher intensity of CO2 generation starting from 0.9 V. In contrast, bare CS only exhibited notable CO2 evolution at 1.4 V, coinciding with the onset of the oxygen evolution reaction. This indicates that MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS not only enabled earlier and more efficient AZN degradation but also suppressed undesirable side reactions. This enhancement can be attributed to the synergistic effect of preconcentration of AZN molecules via the imprinted polymer matrix, and facilitated direct electron transfer enabled by the PBth-BQ conducting layer.

Third, the discharging profiles and corresponding CO2 evolution of both electrodes further illustrated the electrocatalytic advantage of c-MIP in the discharging stage. As shown in Fig. 5c, the OCP of MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS declined more slowly than that of bare CS, correlating with a greater AZN degradation capacity. At potentials ranging from 0.3 to 1.5 V, the CO2 intensity for c-MIP was over five times higher than that of bare CS during both charging and discharging phases, confirming the effective utilization of stored electrical energy for prolonged pollutant oxidation. To further elucidate the electrostatic environment near the electrodes, finite element simulations were conducted. As shown in Fig. 5f, the c-MIP-modified electrode exhibited a stronger and more persistent electric field compared to bare graphite during the discharging phase. This enhancement enabled sustained electrocatalytic oxidation at higher potentials. Additionally, Fig. 5g showed that c-MIP maintained a higher local concentration of SO4 2− anions, which is favorable for charge compensation and ion migration, thereby contributing to its superior OCP retention and electrocatalytic longevity.

A schematic of the proposed mechanism is presented in Fig. 5d, outlining a three-stage process that synergistically regulates both mass and electron flow. The porous, conductive MIP selectively captures ML molecules from the solution through molecular recognition, efficiently preconcentrating them near the electrode surface. Localized enrichment of ECs and enhanced direct electron transfer via PBth-BQ accelerate pollutant oxidation under mild potentials. The high capacitance of the MIP enables electricity storage during charging, which is subsequently released during discharging to drive continued EC degradation. Meanwhile, degradation of ECs regenerates the imprinted cavities for repeated enrichment and oxidation cycles. Together, these results demonstrate that the c-MIP/charging-discharging electrocatalysis platform offers a comprehensive solution for the selective, efficient, and low-energy removal of trace contaminants. By synergistically combining selective enrichment with capacitive discharge-driven electron delivery, this strategy accelerates mass transport and dynamically synchronizes electron flux with reaction kinetics, achieving high-performance degradation that is both scalable and sustainable.

---

## Methods

FTacV measurements
FTacV was performed in a three-electrode system, which consisted of an Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode (in 3 M KCl), a platinum wire as the counter electrode, and the GCE as the working electrode. Bare GCE electrodes were polished with 0.05 μm α-Al2O3 and rinsed with ultrapure water before experiments. Before electrochemical tests, AZN, AMX, CBZ, CIP, and TET were dissolved in 0.1 M Na2SO4 solution, respectively. Using a chi760f workstation (CHI instruments), alternating current voltammetry tests were carried out, in which 256 data points per sine and 65536 data points in total were collected in each test, and the amplitude was set as 0.06 V, with a sensitivity of 10−5 A/V. According to the DPV experiments that have been carried out before, AZN, TET, and AMX were tested at 0~1.2 V, while the CIP and CBZ were tested at 0~1.4 V. For each EC, four tests of 47, 7, 0.977, and 0.19 Hz were carried out.

In-situ DEMS
A state-of-the-art QAS100 DEMS from Linglu Instruments (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., and an Autolab PGSTAT302N (Metrohm, Switzerland) were used to monitor gases and electrochemical signals. A traditional 3-electrode system containing a modified carbon sheet as the working electrode, a Pt wire as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode was applied. The electrolyte consisted of 5 ppm AZN and 0.1 M Na2SO4. An equilibrium of 200 s was performed before electrocatalysis, and the response of 44 amu (CO2) was recorded with PV Mass Spec, and the electrochemical signals were recorded by Nova 2.1.

Preparation of MIP electrodes
A traditional 3-electrode system was applied in electrochemical tests and electro-polymerization, where GCE, graphite carbon plate (GC, 4×2×0.1 cm), or carbon sheet (CS) was used as the working electrode. For the synthesis of MIP(PBth-BQ), 4 mM benzo [1, 2-b; 4, 5-b′] dithiophene-4, 8-dione (Bth-BQ), 2 mM 3, 3′-bithiophene (3, 3′-Bth), 4 mM AZN, 4 mM 3-TBA, and 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium perchlorate were dissolved in acetonitrile. Then cyclic voltammetry was performed with parameters of 0.5–2.3 V vs. non-aqueous Ag+ electrode, 5 cycles, 50 mV/s. For the synthesis of PBth-BQ, 4 mM Bth-BQ was dissolved, and the same CV program was applied.

A pulse procedure was designed to extract templates (AZN) in MIP(PBth-BQ). In a typical run, the potential was set as 1.2 V for 30 s, and then −1.0 V for 30 s. 30 runs were performed in total.

Electrochemical analysis
The discharging test was carried out with a Gamry Interface 1010E in 0.1 M Na2SO4 solution. The MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC, GC, and Ag/AgCl served as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. An OCP procedure was performed with a stirring of 500 rpm after 1.2 V for 60 s. To test the electrochemical capacity of quinone groups, a CV scan of −1.0–0.2 V at 5 mV/s was performed in a N2-saturated solution containing 0.1 M KCl and 0.1 M PBS. The faradic capacity contributed by quinone groups can be calculated with the following equation:

Cquinone = 1/vA * ∫ iPA dt (1)

Here, C is the capacity of quinone in mC/cm2, iPA is the peak current in A, t is the scanning time in s, A is the surface area in cm2, and the result of the integration is the faradic area.

To test the total capacitance of the electrode, a CV scan of 0–0.5 V at 20 mV/s was performed in a N2-saturated solution containing 0.1 M KCl and 0.1 M PBS. The CV curves were converted into i-t curves, and the capacitance was calculated. The total capacitance was calculated with the following equation:

Ctotal = i / (A * v) (2)

To further deconvolute contribution of pseudocapacitance and EDL capacitance, CV scans of electrodes were performed in a N2-saturated solution containing 0.1 M KCl and 0.1 M PBS at 20, 50, 100, and 200 mV/s, respectively.

i(V) = k1v + k2v1/2 (3)

Here, i(V) is the current at a fixed potential (V), v is the scanning rate in mV/s, k1v is the contribution of pseudocapacitive effects, and k2v1/2 is the contribution of diffusion-controlled insertion. The integrated pseudocapacitive response was derived from the fitted k1 and k2 values across the potential range51.

An accelerated lifetime test (ALT) was carried out by charging at 1.2 V for 60 s and then discharging for 120 s. 1000 cycles were repeated in total. FT-IR characterization was performed a on a Vertex 70v/80v (Bruker, Germany) with reflectance mode. The water contact angle was determined and fitted with a LSA60 (LAUDA Scientific, Germany). Atomic force microscope (AFM) test was performed on a MultiMode 8-HR (Bruker, Germany) with a silicon tip on nitride lever (SNL-10), where Scan mode was ScanAsyst in air. SEM tests were performed on a Quanta 250 FEG (FEI, USA) with the high voltage set at 15 kV.

Electrocatalysis
Four 100 mL quartz reactors were used for electrocatalysis at 303 K and 500 rpm. 0.5 mL of the sample was taken from the reactor and filtered with a 0.22 μm membrane prior to analysis. The solid extraction and LC-MS determination were described in Supplementary Note 4. All reported data are presented as mean ± standard deviation from at least three independent replicate measurements (n ≥ 3). 95% confidence intervals were calculated and provided in the supplementary information.

Theoretical calculations
The interaction energy of the mentioned structures was calculated using the ORCA (version 5.0.4) software package. All the calculations were carried out using RI-B3LYP-D3(BJ) function with def2-TZVP basis set. The counterpoise method was used to correct the Basis Set Superposition Error. The Finite Element simulation was performed with COMSOL Multiphysics software.

## Paper

## Abstract

Emerging contaminants (ECs) pose escalating global threats to water security and human health, driving urgent demands for advanced remediation; however, electrocatalytic elimination of trace ECs remains intrinsically constrained by dual limitations: diffusion of ultra-dilute pollutants and sluggish interfacial electron transfer. Here, we introduce an integrated strategy that synergistically regulates mass transport and electron transfer using a conductive molecularly imprinted polymer (c-MIP) electrode operated in a charging-discharging mode. The c-MIP selectively enriches trace ECs at the electrode surface, overcoming diffusion barriers. Critically, its capacitive properties enable temporal control of electron delivery, synchronizing the electron transfer rate with the intrinsic oxidation kinetics of ECs during the discharging phase. This synchronization achieves near-complete EC degradation with 90% lower energy consumption than conventional direct-current electrocatalysis, while maintaining 99% (95% Confidence Interval: 98.0%−100.0%) efficiency over 1,000 cycles. Our work delivers an energy-efficient electrocatalytic platform with operational stability for advanced trace organic pollutant remediation.

---

## Introduction

With the explosive growth of emerging contaminants (ECs) stemming from industrial production and consumer activities, their potential ecological toxicity has become a significant global concern1–5. Although ECs are typically present at trace concentrations, their risk quotients often exceed safety thresholds due to extremely low Predicted No-Effect Concentration, resulting in high ecological risks6–9. In wastewater treatment plants, conventional approaches such as biodegradation and adsorption/membrane filtration are commonly employed for EC removal. However, these methods face significant limitations, including low degradation efficiency and the inability to achieve complete mineralization10,11. Electrocatalysis has emerged as a reliable and adaptable means for advanced water purification12,13. However, its practical application in EC removal is hindered by high energy consumption14. In most cases, substantial overpotentials are required to achieve a satisfactory removal rate, which in turn leads to exponential growth in both energy consumption and carbon emissions15. These challenges underscore the urgent need for innovative electrocatalytic strategies that address both energy efficiency and degradation efficacy.

A key bottleneck in current electrocatalytic systems (Fig. 1) arises from the extremely low concentrations of ECs in wastewater, typically in the ppt-ppm range16–20. Under such conditions, mass transfer of EC molecules from the bulk solution to the electrode surface becomes rate-limiting. Enhancing local reactant concentrations at the electrode-electrolyte interface is therefore critical. Moreover, even if the limitation in mass transfer was overcome, the sluggish electron transfer kinetics in EC degradation also impede performance according to our results. Conventional direct current (DC) electrocatalysis typically expends significant energy overcoming electrode polarization and sustaining undesired side reactions, leading to poor overall energy efficiency21–23. Thus, breaking the limitations in both mass transport and electron transfer simultaneously is the key to improve the energy efficiency of electrocatalytic EC removal.

Selective enrichment of ECs at the electrode surface represents a promising strategy to alleviate mass transport limitations. While many existing strategies focus on overcoming mass transport limitations through selective enrichment, the equally critical constraint of electron transfer kinetics has been largely overlooked. Conventional approaches such as interfacial functionalization or pre-concentration membranes offer limited benefits in enhancing electron transfer process. The integration of molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) and non-potentiostatic electrochemical operation mode offer a compelling solution by simultaneously addressing both challenges. In addition to the high selectivity of MIPs that increases local concentrations of ECs24,25, their porous structures also contribute considerable capacitive properties, allowing them to store electrical energy in the form of non-Faradaic charge within the electrical double layer26–30. Beyond the considerable capacitance, certain long-lived organic radicals formed during catalysis may also contribute to continued contaminant degradation24,25,31. Effectively harnessing this energy presents a novel route to enhance performance and reduce energy input. Therefore, when integrated with appropriate electrochemical operation modes, MIPs can function as electrochemical reservoirs that accumulate charge during DC polarization and gradually release it during the discharging stage. This controlled energy release aligns well with the inherently slow kinetics of EC degradation, thereby enhancing electron transfer efficiency and reducing overall energy consumption.

In this work, we introduce a “charging-discharging” electrocatalytic strategy coupled with a conductive MIP (c-MIP) to synergistically regulate the electron delivery and optimize energy utilization during EC degradation. Using azithromycin (AZN) as a model contaminant, the system achieves significant mineralization in both charging and discharging phases, delivering ~90% energy savings compared to conventional DC electrocatalysis, as confirmed by in-situ CO2 evolution monitored via differential electrochemical mass spectrum (DEMS). Additionally, the system exhibits excellent operational stability, maintaining 99% performance after 1000 cycles. Overall, this work provides a dual-mode electrocatalytic platform that synergistically integrates molecular imprinting and pulse-like energy delivery, offering a scalable, selective, and energy-efficient solution for real-world EC removal in water treatment systems.

---

## Results

Preparing the c-MIP
A thiophene-based c-MIP was prepared using functional monomers as shown in Fig. 2a. It is worth noting that benzo[1,2-b:5,6-b′]dithiophene-4,8-dione (Bth-BQ) was adopted as a redox-active catalytic center to facilitate the direct electron transfer. The electron microscopy images (Supplementary Fig. 1) supported the successful synthesis of c-MIP. To avoid the use of organic reagents like methanol and acetic acid in traditional template extraction32,33, multiple electrochemical extraction methods, potentiostatic, cyclic voltammetry, and redox pulsing, were explored. Then Fe(CN)6 3−/4− was adopted as the redox probe to evaluate the amount of AZN combined with MIP before and after each treatment, as the absence of AZN would improve the accessibility of electrodes to Fe(CN)6 3−/4−. As displayed in Fig. 2b, the reduction peak of Fe(CN)6 3− was suppressed before extraction due to the occlusion of surface sites by AZN. The reduction peak rose after all 5 procedures, and the redox pulses switched between 1.2 V for 30 s and −1.0 V for 30 s (Fig. 2c) performed best as the peak current boosted most. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) corroborated these findings. The Nyquist plots of the MIP (PBth-BQ)@GCE before and after pulsed extraction differed a lot (Supplementary Fig. 2a). By fitting parameters with the equivalent-circuit model shown in Supplementary Fig. 2b, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) of MIP dropped from 4358.0 ± 98.8 Ω to 60.9 ± 7.0 Ω after extracting AZN templates by the redox pulse, indicating a more accessible interface for electron transfer. Also, the fitted n dropped from 0.92 ± 0.01 to 0.63 ± 0.02 after extracting templates, indicating enhanced surface porosity34.

To further confirm the successful imprinting and removal of AZN, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis was conducted. A prominent absorption at ~1630 cm−1, corresponding to the C=O stretching of AZN35, was present in the MIP before extraction and disappeared following redox pulsing (Fig. 2d). Upon rebinding AZN, the C=O peak re-emerged, verifying the selective recognition capability of the MIP without structural degradation. As revealed by contact angle measurements, an improved hydrophilicity was achieved after polymerization, decreasing from 89.1 ± 3.9° to 43.2 ± 2.3° (Fig. 2e), which is expected to promote aqueous-phase contaminant capture36. Also, a thin and uniform MIP layer is crucial for the selective recognition and rapid adsorption of target ECs, as the uptake process primarily follows a Langmuir-type mechanism involving monolayer adsorption onto a limited number of imprinted sites. An excessively thick MIP layer may hinder the direct electron transfer between the captured ECs and the underlying electrode surface by increasing charge transfer resistance and limiting access to electroactive sites. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis confirmed a uniform film morphology with a thickness of approximately ~7 nm (Fig. 2f, g), indicating a favorable two-dimensional configuration for electron transport37,38. The AZN adsorption isotherm on c-MIP (Supplementary Fig. 3) showed a maximum adsorption capacity (qm) of 16.35 μg/cm2 and demonstrated a Langmuir-type adsorption behavior (R2=0.99), which indicated a single layer adsorption. As a result, the adsorption kinetics tests demonstrated the rapid and high-capacity uptake of AZN by the MIP (PBth-BQ)@GC electrode that it adsorbed 8.4 times more AZN than bare GC in 10 min and 6.8 times more in 240 min (Fig. 2h).

Identifying electron transfer limitation of ECs beyond mass transport
To identify electron transfer behaviors of typical ECs in electrochemical oxidation, we employed Fourier-transform alternating current voltammetry (FTacV) to evaluate five typical ECs: AZN, carbamazepine (CBZ), tetracycline (TET), amoxicillin (AMX), and ciprofloxacin (CIP). The ECs are dripped on the glassy carbon electrode (GCE) to avoid diffusion limitation. The total current, AC voltammetry (ACV), direct current voltammetry, and 3rd harmonic components extracted from FTacV measurements on a bare GCE in the presence and absence of each EC were displayed in Supplementary Figs. 4–9. Generally, the 3rd harmonic ACV excluded the contribution of non-faradic current and decoupled overlapping electron transfer processes, thereby offering deeper insights into the redox behaviors of these ECs. Notably, the 3rd harmonic ACV current responses recorded at varying frequencies (0.19–47 Hz) suggested the difference in electron transfer rates of these ECs39,40.

Among the ECs tested, AZN, a macrolide antibiotic of significant environmental concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial activity41, exhibited the slowest electron transfer kinetics. At a high frequency of 47 Hz, AZN displayed a weak oxidation signal between 0.5 and 1.0 V (Fig. 3a). However, as the frequency decreased, the oxidation peak increased markedly, suggesting a strong dependence on electron transfer rate42. This trend reflects the sluggish redox kinetics of AZN, which is further corroborated by the monotonic increase of normalized third harmonic current (I3/f) with decreasing frequency. A similar trend was observed for AMX, CBZ, CIP, and TET, indicating that electron transfer limitation is a common bottleneck in the electrochemical oxidation of ECs. These observations collectively suggest that most ECs in wastewater are characterized by inherently slow interfacial electron transfer processes. Meanwhile, their trace concentrations (ppt-ppm) impose significant mass transfer limitations, reducing the flux of reactants to the electrode surface. These two limitations act in concert that the insufficient delivery of ECs exacerbates the already sluggish electron transfer kinetics, resulting in low overall reaction rates. As a result, in conventional electrochemical degradation systems, only a small portion of the input electrical energy contributes directly to pollutant removal, while the majority is dissipated to overcome polarization and maintain the electric double layer. Recognizing the dual constraints imposed by mass and electron transfer, we selected AZN, a typical macrolide antibiotic (ML), as a representative EC due to its environmental relevance and characteristically slow degradation kinetics, which enables a focused investigation of strategies aimed at improving electrocatalytic performance and energy efficiency.

Overcoming the mismatch of electron flow with sluggish electron transfer of ECs
To elucidate the potential of discharging induced degradation of ECs, DEMS was employed to monitor the real-time evolution of gaseous products near the working electrode. As shown in Fig. 4a, the relative intensity of CO2 increased steadily during the potentiostatic “charging” phase (applied for 300 s), indicating active mineralization of AZN under applied potential. Control experiments (Supplementary Fig. 10) confirmed that the origin of the CO2 signal. In the absence of AZN, the CO2 intensity decreased by 96%, verifying that the detected CO2 primarily arose from AZN mineralization rather than background sources. A minor residual CO2 signal was attributed to the decomposition of the Vaseline used for sealing the DEMS cell. Intriguingly, during the subsequent “discharging” phase under open-circuit, the CO2 signal continued to rise transiently despite the cessation of external voltage. This delayed decline (Δt≈30 s) in CO2 intensity implies that the stored charge within the porous electrode or the electrical double layer sustained further mineralization of AZN even in the absence of an applied potential. To further validate this coupling between stored charge and continued degradation, a series of time-dependent experiments were conducted following different durations of the charging phase (Supplementary Fig. 11). In particular, a brief closed-circuit pulse (0 V, 1 s) was introduced after potentiostatic charging to consume the stored charge, and a sharp decrease in CO2 intensity was observed. This confirms that the stored electrical energy in the electrode and interfacial regions could be effectively released to drive continued AZN mineralization during discharging stage.

To demonstrate the compatibility of c-MIP with the charging-discharging operation mode, its capacitive characteristics were thoroughly investigated. Capacitance fitting based on EIS (Supplementary Fig. 12) revealed a film capacitance (Cfilm) of 2701 ± 773 μF and an electrical double layer capacitance (CEDL) of 12.2 ± 1.4 μF. Differential capacitance analysis by cyclic voltammetry attributed most of the increased faradaic capacitance to quinone groups (Supplementary Fig. 13), whereas PBth-BQ contributed minimally to non-faradaic capacitance. The substantial enhancement in total capacitance (Fig. 4b) was attributed to the porous MIP structure, as supported by BET analysis that the specific surface area increased from 3.28 m2/g to 47.25 m2/g, and pore volume also rose markedly (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15). To further clarify the origin of capacitance enhancement, the total capacitance was deconvoluted into pseudocapacitive and EDL components and correlated with surface area and pore structure (Supplementary Fig. 17). After electropolymerization, the surface area decreased, and CEDL declined due to the coverage of the dense polymer layer, while a distinct pseudocapacitive response emerged from the introduced quinone redox sites. After extracting templates, both the surface area and pore connectivity increased, accompanied by a pronounced rise in CEDL and a moderate increase in Cpseudo. The pore-sized distribution was centered around 2.6 nm, within the mesopore range, consistent with the enhanced ion-accessible channels that promoted double-layer formation. These trends indicated that the enhanced pore accessibility mainly promoted double-layer formation, while the pseudocapacitance was controlled by the density of exposed redox-active sites. Moreover, the adsorption capacity normalized by surface area exhibited a consistent increase, supporting that improved pore connectivity facilitated pollutant enrichment and charge utilization (Supplementary Fig. 17f). Impressively, the MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC electrode delivered superior continuous discharging performance. As shown in Fig. 4c, discharging curves were collected for various electrodes after a 60-s potentiostatic charging step in 0.1 M Na2SO4. The modification of PBth-BQ resulted in a slower decay in voltage, indicative of enhanced charge retention or higher capacitance. Notably, the discharging duration was significantly extended even in low-electrolyte conditions (0.005 M Na2SO4), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18. Furthermore, kinetic analysis of PBth-BQ yielded a discharging rate constant (k0’) of 0.216 s−1 (Supplementary Fig. 19), supporting its long-lived redox activity. Moreover, this strategy was validated on alternative substrates, that PBth-BQ and MIP(PBth-BQ) also significantly enhanced the discharging behavior of titanium-based electrodes (Fig. 4c), highlighting its general applicability. Thus, the conductive and porous nature of MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC not only promotes selective AZN adsorption but also acts as temporary energy reservoirs for sustained contaminant degradation. This dual role supports a charging-discharging electrocatalytic degradation pathway, whereby more electrons are stored during the charging stage and subsequently released in a sustained manner during discharging, enabling effective degradation of MLs.

Equipped with capacitive c-MIP, we conducted a series of charging-discharging experiments for energy-efficient pollutants removal. As illustrated in Fig. 4e, the electrode adsorbed approximately 50% of AZN within 1 h via selective binding to imprinted cavities. Upon subsequent DC electrolysis at 1.2 V, 98% of AZN was effectively degraded. Surprisingly, a cyclic “charging-discharging” mode, which introduced a 2-min discharging stage after each charging cycle, achieved comparable removal efficiency to the continuous DC mode, despite reducing the total “circuit-on” time by 66.7%, indicating substantial energy savings. By employing denser sampling during the discharge period, we further confirmed that AZN was substantially degraded in the discharging stage itself (Supplementary Fig. 20a). In contrast, a control charging-pulse procedure that disabled the discharging phase (gray line in Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 20) resulted in much lower removal rates, underscoring the critical role of discharging-associated catalysis. The discharging curves remained stable over 80 cycles, with OCP decreasing gradually from 1.2 V to 0.9 V (Fig. 4d). The subtle change of OCP caused by AZN (Supplementary Fig. 21) suggested that the adsorption of ECs had little effect on the discharging processes. The high efficiency of AZN degradation at lower potentials was corroborated by differential pulse voltammetry (DPV, Supplementary Fig. 22), showing superior activity of MIP(PBth-BQ)@GC over bare GC, attributed to both enhanced AZN enrichment by the MIP and efficient direct electron transfer facilitated by Bth-BQ. The degradation activity exhibited negligible decline even as the OCP decreased to 0.9 V, implying the limited electron transfer in electrochemical oxidation of ECs. Further insights from Supplementary Fig. 23 confirmed that AZN oxidation primarily occurred between 0.7 and 1.4 V, aligning with DEMS data (Supplementary Fig. 24), where CO2 evolution initiated at 0.7 V and remained stable between 0.9 and 1.2 V, supporting sustained mineralization of AZN in the discharging phase.

In terms of durability, the electrode retained its electrochemical capacitance over 1000 continuous charging-discharging cycles (Fig. 4f), and maintained structural integrity throughout a 14-day accelerated lifetime test. Detailed capacity retention behavior over 1000 discharging cycles, as well as FTIR, XPS, and SEM analyses before and after extended cycling, are provided in Supplementary Figs. 25 and 26, confirming the long-term stability of the c-MIP electrode. Nyquist plots and fitted parameters (Rct and n, Supplementary Fig. 27b, c) further validated the long-term stability of the c-MIP architecture. To assess the limits of electron utilization, a prolonged discharging protocol, a 19-min discharging period followed a 1-min charging cycle, was employed, in which the OCP declined from 1.2 V to 0.6 V (Fig. 4g). Although the degradation rate constant decreased at lower potentials, the final AZN removal remained high. In 12 full cycles, the terminal discharging potential stabilized, demonstrating consistency in performance. While the charging-discharging electrocatalysis displayed slightly slower kinetics than DC electrolysis, the final removal rate was comparable (Fig. 4h). In contrast, the gray curve (charging-discharging 3#) concentrated all charging periods at the beginning rather than distributing them cyclically, thereby losing the benefit of alternating charge-discharge regulation and resulting in weaker degradation efficiency. The gray controls in Fig. 4e and h, though configured differently, showed the same discharge suppression and similarly reduced performance. These results collectively confirmed that the cyclic distribution of charging and discharging stages was essential for maintaining high removal efficiency. To further verify the effectiveness of this process at the mineralization level, total organic carbon (TOC) and ion chromatography (IC) analyses were performed. TOC and AZN concentrations decreased simultaneously in the initial adsorption stage (Supplementary Fig. 29), confirming rapid enrichment by the c-MIP electrode. During the charging-discharging stage, TOC exhibited a short-term increase that may be attributed to the release of oxidized intermediates into solution, followed by a steady decline as these species were further degraded. After 5 h, 79.0% ± 2.6% of TOC was removed (95% CI: 74.1%–83.9%), and IC analysis confirmed the absence of NO3−, suggesting substantial mineralization of AZN. LC-MS further indicated that key intermediate products of AZN exhibited reduced toxicity (Supplementary Figs. 30 and 31). Strikingly, energy consumption was dramatically lower that DC electrolysis consumed 35.85 ± 0.55 C to degrade 97.6 ± 0.17% of AZN in 5 h, whereas charging-discharging electrocatalysis achieved 96.7 ± 0.01% degradation using only 3.76 ± 0.19 C, or 10.5 ± 0.4% (95% Confidence Interval: 9.4%–11.6%) of the energy required by the DC mode (Fig. 4i and Supplementary Table 3). The substantial energy savings primarily stem from the synergistic contribution of the c-MIP and the charging-discharging operation, where electrical energy is stored temporarily at the charging stages and then released at the discharge stages, emulating reservoir-like energy redistribution. This process effectively reduces energy dissipation that would otherwise be spent on sustaining electrode polarization and maintaining the electric double layer in continuous DC systems.

To further examine the practical applicability of c-MIP coupled with charging-discharging electrocatalysis, the removal of AZN was tested in lower concentrations and in real water samples. C-MIP captured 45.2, 68.5, and 86.7% of AZN in 60 min when the initial concentration were 5 ppm, 1 ppm, and 0.5 ppm, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 32). At lower initial concentrations, c-MIP coupled with charging-discharging electrocatalysis achieved more effective AZN removal, in which selective adsorption demonstrated remarkable capability of selective adsorption for rapidly enriching the target analyte, especially from dilute solutions. In real water samples, the enrichment of AZN by c-MIP was slightly affected, as the removal rate within 60 min decreased from 47.2% in synthetic water to 36.3% and 40.3% in two real water samples (Supplementary Fig. 33a). This decline can be attributed to the interferences from natural organic matters containing hydroxyl groups. The selectivity of c-MIP toward AZN over other three coexisting ECs in real water was also examined, where c-MIP maintained a high selectivity of 75.6%–87.0% (Supplementary Fig. 34). The charging-discharging processes were also influenced in real water, with lower OCP values during discharging process compared with synthetic systems (Supplementary Fig. 34b), which may be attributed to the low conductivity of real matrices. Consequently, the final AZN removal rate after 5 h decreased from 96.7% in synthetic water to 86.2% and 88.5% in real samples, while electricity consumption also dropped from 3.76 ± 0.19 C to 0.39 ± 0.06 C and 0.48 ± 0.01 C, respectively, indicating high energy efficiency.

Furthermore, the c-MIP platform was extended to validate its capability for selectively enriching diverse ECs. For ECs containing hydroxyl groups like TET, a c-MIP was constructed using 3-TBA as the functional monomer, enabling the formation of boronate ester bonds with hydroxyl groups of TET (Supplementary Fig. 35a). The resulting c-MIP exhibited strong selectivity toward TET (Supplementary Fig. 35b), with minimal interference from DCF and SMX. Similarly, for ECs containing carboxyl groups like DCF, 3,4-diaminothiophene (3,4-NH2-Th) was employed as the functional monomer to form amide bonds (Supplementary Fig. 35c). Although its overall efficiency was slightly inferior to the c-MIPs developed for MLs and TET (Supplementary Fig. 35d), these results confirm that amide bond formation is a viable strategy for imprinting carboxyl-containing contaminants. However, targeting amino-group-containing ECs such as SMX proved more challenging. A c-MIP prepared with 3,4-thiophenedicarboxylic acid as the functional monomer was designed to form amide bonds with SMX (Supplementary Fig. 35e), while the resulting polymer failed to effectively distinguish SMX from TET (Supplementary Fig. 35f). This reduced selectivity can be attributed to the slower kinetics of amide bond formation with amino groups, while TET, bearing multiple hydroxyl groups, rapidly formed stable boronate esters, thereby outcompeting SMX and dominating the binding sites. Taken together, these results indicated that the c-MIP strategy can be readily adapted by tailoring template molecules and selecting complementary functional monomers, thereby enabling selective enrichment of ECs containing hydroxyl or carboxyl functional groups.

To address safety concerns in large-scale applications, specifically the instantaneous current surge associated with constant-voltage (CV) charging, a constant-current-constant-voltage (CCCV) protocol was adopted, inspired by battery technologies43. A cut-off potential of 1.65 V was set to avoid oxygen evolution, as determined by LSV analysis (Supplementary Fig. 36). A constant charging current of 0.07 A was identified as optimal, taking ~20 s to reach the cut-off voltage (Supplementary Fig. 37). Compared to the CV-only method, which reached a peak current of 380 mA, the CCCV protocol peaked at a much lower 70 mA (Fig. 4j), reducing surge-related risks while maintaining degradation performance (Supplementary Fig. 38). Leveraging this optimized procedure, we scaled up the system to a 5 L reactor to assess practical feasibility (Fig. 4k). Despite the increased volume, efficient AZN degradation with low energy input was maintained (Supplementary Fig. 40). The slight drop in removal efficiency was primarily attributed to mass transfer limitations stemming from suboptimal mixing. The radar chart displayed in Fig. 4l summarizes the comprehensive advantages of c-MIP and pulsed electrocatalysis across multiple performance indicators. Compared to PBth-BQ-modified electrodes, the c-MIP system demonstrated superior adsorption capacity, selectivity, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, charging-discharging electrocatalysis outperformed the DC mode in terms of cycling stability and power economy. Although pulsed electrocatalysis has been explored in contexts such as CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR)44–47 and redox-active electrode stability48,49, its application of “charging-discharging” as a strategy for energy-saving electrocatalysis remains largely unexplored. Our work pioneers this approach, demonstrating that the synergistic integration of c-MIP and charging-discharging electrocatalysis can significantly break the binary constraints of mass transport and electron transfer when addressing trace ECs, offering a promising paradigm for sustainable environmental remediation.

Mechanism of the efficient electrocatalytic removal of targeted ECs
To elucidate the underlying mechanism behind the efficient and energy-saving electrocatalytic degradation of MLs, we further examined the mass and electron transfer dynamics of charging-discharging electrocatalysis using c-MIP electrodes. We first evaluated the targeted mass transfer behavior of c-MIP by testing five ECs. Namely, three target MLs, AZN, roxithromycin (ROX), and clarithromycin (CLA), and two common interferences, TET and CBZ. As shown in Fig. 5a, the c-MIP electrode selectively enriched the targeted MLs from the bulk solution, confirming its molecular recognition ability. To further clarify the driving factors enabling dilute contaminants to approach the electrode surface, adsorption experiments of AZN were conducted under different stirring rates (0–1000 rpm) and initial concentrations (0.5–10 ppm). Higher stirring rates significantly accelerated adsorption kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 41), indicating that external mass transfer was important in dilute systems, while the adsorption capacity increased with concentration, confirming the concentration gradient as the primary driving force. These results provided direct evidence supporting the effective enrichment of trace pollutants by c-MIP electrodes, beyond the molecular recognition effect. More importantly, beyond these generic effects, c-MIP provided a unique advantage over conventional adsorption materials. The imprinted sites can form reversible covalent linkages with target molecules, enabling rapid capture and suppressing desorption, thereby shifting the adsorption-desorption equilibrium toward efficient enrichment. To understand the interaction at a molecular level, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to estimate the binding energies between thiopheneboronic acid (TBA) and the three ECs (Fig. 5e). Among them, AZN exhibited the strongest binding affinity with TBA at −5.34 eV, which likely arises from the boric acid-cis-diol interaction, a highly specific covalent interaction. This selectivity was further reinforced by the “lock-and-key recognition” effect inherent to the spatial structure of the MIP matrix50. Although TET and CBZ also formed interactions with TBA, their calculated binding energies were weaker than that of AZN, yet still stronger than non-specific adsorption on graphite (−0.81 eV), possibly due to boric acid-hydroxyl group bonding.

Second, to probe the electrochemical degradation in the charging stage, in-situ DEMS was employed. During LSV, the evolution profiles and LSV currents of MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS and bare CS were compared (Fig. 5b). MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS showed significantly higher current between 0.7 and 1.4 V, correlating with the earlier onset and higher intensity of CO2 generation starting from 0.9 V. In contrast, bare CS only exhibited notable CO2 evolution at 1.4 V, coinciding with the onset of the oxygen evolution reaction. This indicates that MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS not only enabled earlier and more efficient AZN degradation but also suppressed undesirable side reactions. This enhancement can be attributed to the synergistic effect of preconcentration of AZN molecules via the imprinted polymer matrix, and facilitated direct electron transfer enabled by the PBth-BQ conducting layer.

Third, the discharging profiles and corresponding CO2 evolution of both electrodes further illustrated the electrocatalytic advantage of c-MIP in the discharging stage. As shown in Fig. 5c, the OCP of MIP(PBth-BQ)@CS declined more slowly than that of bare CS, correlating with a greater AZN degradation capacity. At potentials ranging from 0.3 to 1.5 V, the CO2 intensity for c-MIP was over five times higher than that of bare CS during both charging and discharging phases, confirming the effective utilization of stored electrical energy for prolonged pollutant oxidation. To further elucidate the electrostatic environment near the electrodes, finite element simulations were conducted. As shown in Fig. 5f, the c-MIP-modified electrode exhibited a stronger and more persistent electric field compared to bare graphite during the discharging phase. This enhancement enabled sustained electrocatalytic oxidation at higher potentials. Additionally, Fig. 5g showed that c-MIP maintained a higher local concentration of SO4 2− anions, which is favorable for charge compensation and ion migration, thereby contributing to its superior OCP retention and electrocatalytic longevity.

A schematic of the proposed mechanism is presented in Fig. 5d, outlining a three-stage process that synergistically regulates both mass and electron flow. The porous, conductive MIP selectively captures ML molecules from the solution through molecular recognition, efficiently preconcentrating them near the electrode surface. Localized enrichment of ECs and enhanced direct electron transfer via PBth-BQ accelerate pollutant oxidation under mild potentials. The high capacitance of the MIP enables electricity storage during charging, which is subsequently released during discharging to drive continued EC degradation. Meanwhile, degradation of ECs regenerates the imprinted cavities for repeated enrichment and oxidation cycles. Together, these results demonstrate that the c-MIP/charging-discharging electrocatalysis platform offers a comprehensive solution for the selective, efficient, and low-energy removal of trace contaminants. By synergistically combining selective enrichment with capacitive discharge-driven electron delivery, this strategy accelerates mass transport and dynamically synchronizes electron flux with reaction kinetics, achieving high-performance degradation that is both scalable and sustainable.
